title: Richard Kieckhefer Publishes Magic in the Middle Ages
description:
Richard Kieckhefer's Magic in the Middle Ages, first published in 1976 and revised in a second edition in 1989, was a foundational scholarly rehabilitation of medieval magic as a legitimate subject of serious historical inquiry. Kieckhefer, a historian of medieval religion at Northwestern University, approached magic not as primitive irrationality but as a coherent set of beliefs and practices embedded in medieval religious and intellectual culture. The book distinguished between different categories of medieval magic — natural magic, astral magic, demonic magic, and folk magic — and traced how these categories were defined, contested, and institutionally managed across the medieval period.

Kieckhefer's concept of the 'common tradition' — the stratum of practical magic shared across social levels, distinct from both the learned necromancy of university-trained clergymen and the formal theology of inquisitors — was particularly influential. It provided a framework for understanding how magic was distributed across society in ways that cut across the elite/popular divide that older scholarship had emphasized. His analysis of how the cumulative concept of witchcraft was constructed through a series of intellectual steps between roughly 1370 and 1450 — combining pre-existing elements of maleficium, diabolical pact, and sabbath — remains the standard account of how the prosecuted witchcraft of the early modern period came into being.

The broader influence of Magic in the Middle Ages extended beyond witchcraft studies into the history of medieval religion, popular belief, and the sociology of knowledge. Kieckhefer's subsequent work, including Forbidden Rites (1997, on a fifteenth-century necromancer's manual) and Magic and Religion in the Middle Ages (2000), extended his framework across different aspects of medieval magical culture.
historiographical_note: Kieckhefer's work is treated as foundational by virtually all subsequent scholars of medieval magic and early modern witchcraft. His analysis of the construction of the 'cumulative concept of witchcraft' in the late fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries provides the intellectual-historical context for understanding the Alpine trials that first put this concept into judicial practice. Stuart Clark's intellectual history draws on Kieckhefer's framework for the medieval background to early modern demonology. Brian Levack's chronological framing of the witch-hunt places its beginning in the period Kieckhefer identified as crucial.
source_method: Primary scholarship (Kieckhefer, Magic in the Middle Ages, 1976/1989); subsequent scholarly responses
